clue.text: Maiden in reverse initially denting bumper?

indicators.note: Taken at the very start, so only the letter that opens the neighbouring word is wanted.
A dent is a push into a surface, so one letter is driven inside the other piece.

blocks.note: the initial letter of the word, and nothing else of it
a bumper is something that bumps, and the hand you bump is a fist — the question mark owns the stretch

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a car-park prang: reversing, denting, bumpers. Underneath, every one of those words has been given a different job.
explanation.definitionFit: Maiden → FIRST: a maiden voyage, a maiden century, a maiden speech — 'maiden' is the adjective English keeps for the earliest of its kind.

clue.text: Doing this, not going to multiply 24?

blocks.clueFragment: Doing this, not going to multiply
blocks.note: The surface offers arithmetic, a sum you are declining to do. The setter means the other multiplying, the biblical be-fruitful kind, and a cartridge with no bullet in it.
A number this far from any arithmetic is a cross-reference: solve 24 across and you have the second joke, because a cartridge like that makes a report that is doing none of a shot's work.

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference earns its keep twice. As a figure it belongs to the sum the surface pretends to set; as a signpost it sends you off to another entry for the punchline.
explanation.definitionFit: not going to multiply → FIRING BLANKS: 'multiply' is the be-fruitful sense, and a blank round carries no bullet, so nothing is conceived.

clue.text: Bird tough for Archer

blocks.note: the red-breasted garden bird of every British Christmas card
a hood is a hoodlum, a street heavy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Archer' is the misdirection and the definition at the same time: the surface offers Jeffrey Archer the novelist, and the clue wants a man with a bow.
explanation.definitionFit: Archer → ROBIN HOOD: definition by example — the Sherwood outlaw is the bowman everyone names, so one famous figure stands in for the whole class.

clue.text: One south of flipping green district of Rome

indicators.note: Flip something and it lands the other way up, so the letters that follow are read from their far end.
This entry runs down the grid, so whatever is south of another piece is written underneath it.

blocks.note: vert is the heraldic name for green, the colour as a coat of arms gives it
the Roman numeral, which is where the surface has been standing all along

explanation.walkthrough: Heraldry is worth learning as a source of colours: vert, gules, azure and sable turn up constantly and almost never mean anything else.
explanation.definitionFit: district of Rome → TREVI: one of the city's rioni, the historic administrative districts, and the one that gives the famous fountain its name.

clue.text: Italian food with taste of cheese a plebeian’s thrown about

indicators.note: A taste is a small helping out of a larger portion, so only part of what follows is being served.
Thrown about, a run of letters ends up facing the opposite way and is read from its far end.

blocks.note: eight letters sit consecutively here, starting three into the first word and stopping short of the last two — then they are read the other way

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is that this looks like an anagram, with 'thrown about' begging you to shuffle. Nothing is shuffled: the letters are already in the clue, in order, running backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian food → BEL PAESE: a mild cow's-milk cheese from Lombardy sold under exactly that name, which in Italian means 'beautiful country'.

clue.text: It’s rolled over, in something to kick – and pass

indicators.note: Roll something over and it comes to rest the opposite way up, so those letters go down backwards.
Plain as it looks, this little word is the instruction: one group of letters is dropped inside another.

blocks.note: kick the bucket — the thing kicked is the one in the idiom, not the one on a football pitch
the two words shrink to three letters, then turn round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Something to kick' pulls hard towards a ball, and the answer needs the dying idiom instead.
explanation.definitionFit: pass → BUS TICKET: a pass is any slip that buys you entry or travel, and the fare paid to ride is one everyday instance.

clue.text: Opera, not entirely mirthful, ultimately uplifting

indicators.note: Only a portion of what follows is wanted — a run taken out of the middle, never the whole words.
This entry runs down the grid, so anything lifted up is read from the bottom of the run back to the top.

blocks.note: four letters run straight across the gap between these two words, comma and all

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' reads as an order to take a last letter, and that is the trap. It is fodder: the answer is buried across it and the word in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera → LULU: Alban Berg's unfinished twelve-tone opera, four letters long and therefore a fixture of crossword grids everywhere.

clue.text: Other toad in soup, here

indicators.note: To be in the soup is to be in a mess, and letters in a mess have lost the order they were given in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is a witch's cauldron and not one word of it suggests a house, which is why the small definition at the end looks like an afterthought.
explanation.definitionFit: here → AT THE DOOR: a caller announced as 'here' is standing on the step outside, so the vague word names one particular spot.

clue.text: Fight to draw up, through case in scabbard – this?

indicators.note: Drawn up, a piece travels towards the top of the column, so its letters are read upwards.
Going through something means passing inside it, so one piece is threaded into the middle of another.
A case is the shell round a thing, so only the two letters at the outside of the word are kept.

blocks.note: the outermost letters of the word, the casing with the middle thrown away
a row is a fight, a shouting quarrel

explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' belongs to the fight on the surface and to the sheath underneath, since drawing is what you do to a blade. That double life is what hides the turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: this? → SWORD: the definition points back at the clue's own picture — what a scabbard holds is the blade, and 'this' asks you to name it.

clue.text: Sticky stuff, something to fill squares alongside something to remove it?

indicators.note: It says only that the two halves sit next to each other; which of them comes first is left to the enumeration.

blocks.note: in British English the thing that takes pencil off paper is a rubber, what Americans call an eraser
the completed answers to a crossword are its solution

explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes the object in your hands: pencil in the grid, rub it out again. Only 'Sticky stuff' is looking anywhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: Sticky stuff → RUBBER SOLUTION: the rubber cement in a bicycle puncture-repair kit is sold under that exact name, and it is glue.

clue.text: Planet in stew, for troubled – don’t expect it to get better!

definitions.text: don’t expect it to get better!

indicators.note: Troubled water is churned up and unsettled, and letters in that state have lost their order.

blocks.note: the planet we are standing on, spelled out in full
the word goes into the mix at face value, all four letters
three more letters lifted straight off the page

explanation.walkthrough: 'Planet in stew' reads as an insertion, something dropped into the pot, and it is nothing of the kind: the planet's five letters are shuffled along with the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: don’t expect it to get better! → FEAR THE WORST: the idiom is an instruction to brace for the bad outcome instead of hoping for a good one.

clue.text: Elastic on equipment in racket pulled back

indicators.note: The smallest word in the clue is the instruction: what comes before it goes inside what comes after.
An across answer reversed reads right to left, and pulling a thing back is exactly that about-turn.

blocks.note: a racket is a din, and the din is turned round to make the shell
two letters taken straight off the page
a rig is equipment: a drilling rig, a lighting rig

explanation.walkthrough: Every noun here belongs to a tennis club — elastic, equipment, racket — and 'racket' is the one that changes sense, from the thing you swing to the noise you make.
explanation.definitionFit: Elastic → NON-RIGID: elastic in its adjectival sense means yielding and able to bend, which is precisely what a thing that will not stay stiff does.

clue.text: Bait in hand?

blocks.note: the verb, not the worm: to bait somebody is to keep poking at them until they rise to it
the second half is a picture rather than a synonym — the thin sharp thing a knitter, a tailor or a nurse is holding — and the question mark admits as much

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, no wordplay, two runs at the same answer. Short clues like this are often the last ones in, because there is nothing to take apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Bait → NEEDLE is to goad or provoke; 'in hand?' asks for the object itself, the slim steel spike you hold to sew, knit or inject.

clue.text: Prize to catch shark detailed – one taking bets

indicators.note: To catch a thing is to close your hand round it, so one piece shuts around the other.
Read it as de-tailed rather than itemised: the tail comes off the word it follows.

blocks.note: the Booker is Britain's best-known literary prize, awarded each year to a novel
a mako is a fast open-sea shark, and de-tailed it loses its closing O

explanation.walkthrough: 'Prize to catch' reads as the start of a definition, something worth landing, and 'Prize' is really a proper noun with a hole cut in it.
explanation.definitionFit: one taking bets → BOOKMAKER: the trade name for someone who makes a book on a race, holding the stakes and paying out the winners.

clue.text: Flash activated, faint shiner

blocks.note: in a flash and in a mo both mean in a moment
a switch that has been activated is on
light rain, a light breeze: light does duty for faint

explanation.walkthrough: 'Faint shiner' looks like the definition and is one word too long. 'Faint' has already been spent on the last chunk of the build.
explanation.definitionFit: shiner → MOONLIGHT: the setter names the thing by what it does, and what shines down on a clear night is the pale borrowed glow of the moon.

clue.text: Part played by Baltic capital investing millions in bureaucracy

indicators.note: To invest is to put money into a thing, and the letters go the same way: one piece placed inside another.

blocks.note: the capital of Latvia, one of the three Baltic states
m is the standard shortening for millions on any balance sheet
the part an actor plays is their role

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a government pouring millions into red tape, and the answer is the red tape. A definition that agrees with the picture is the hardest kind to notice.
explanation.definitionFit: bureaucracy → RIGMAROLE: a long-winded procedure full of pointless steps, which is what people are complaining about when they use the drier word.

clue.text: Award unblemished?

blocks.note: unblemished means there is not one on you, and that 'no' is written as the O that stands for nothing
the blemish being denied is the mark a healed wound leaves behind

explanation.walkthrough: One word of wordplay, and it has to be heard rather than dissected: 'unblemished' is being read as a two-word phrase meaning the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Award → OSCAR: definition by example — the Academy's gold statuette is one particular prize standing here for the whole category.

clue.text: Tripped, breaking item of crockery – in little pieces?

indicators.note: Breaking into a house means getting inside it, so one word is prised open and the other put in.

blocks.note: the everyday item of crockery, and here it gets split open
to trip along is to move in light quick steps, which is to hop

explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking ... crockery' is a picture and an instruction at once: the crockery really is broken in two, and the other word is put in the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: in little pieces? → CHOPPED UP: a cook reduces an onion to small bits by chopping, and the phrase names that end state rather than the act.

clue.text: Sound German wheels round

blocks.note: the car marque from Ingolstadt, four letters of German engineering
a round drawn on the page is the letter O

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' at the front of a clue almost always asks you to listen. Here it is simply the definition, and nothing in this one is being said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Sound → AUDIO: the noun for recorded or transmitted sound, the audio of a broadcast as against its video.

clue.text: Old plane flying right to me

indicators.note: Letters in flight are letters off the ground and out of place, and the word doubles as what the thing defined actually does.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is also the scenery. A plane flying is what the surface describes, so 'flying' reads as description rather than as the order it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Old plane → TIGER MOTH: the de Havilland biplane that trained RAF pilots in the 1930s, so one particular aircraft answers a general description.

clue.text: Empty lounge behind warm fire

indicators.note: Emptied out, a word keeps only the letters at its two ends and loses everything between them.
Whatever is behind something follows it, so this piece is written after the other, not before.

blocks.note: the human sense of warm, said of a person rather than a temperature
the two outside letters of the word, with OUNG gone from the middle

explanation.walkthrough: Read straight it describes a room — an empty lounge, a warm fire — and every word of that picture is quietly carrying an instruction instead.
explanation.definitionFit: fire → KINDLE: both are verbs for getting a blaze going, and English fires and kindles enthusiasm in exactly the same figurative way.

clue.text: Under orderly, hospital

blocks.note: an orderly desk is a tidy one: the adjective, not the hospital porter the surface offers
H is the standard abbreviation on maps and road signs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Orderly, hospital' reads as one idea, the man wheeling the trolleys, and is two pieces underneath. The answer is a poetic clipping that drops the be- from beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Under → NEATH: the poetic contraction of beneath, doing in a line of verse the job that 'under' does in prose.

clue.text: Was sad about having caged a parrot? So get a perch

indicators.note: Turned about, a word faces the other way, so those four letters are entered from the back.
A cage holds its occupant inside, so one group of letters shuts around the other.

blocks.note: someone sad wept, and the word goes down back to front
the kea is a large green parrot from the New Zealand mountains, and the 'a' comes along with it

explanation.walkthrough: Parrot, caged, perch: the birds run right through to the last word, and the answer has nothing to do with birds at all.
explanation.definitionFit: get a perch → TAKE A PEW: a pew is the long bench in a church, so an invitation to take one is the English way of saying sit down.

clue.text: Little bit topped with last of chocolate, lay it on thick

indicators.note: This entry runs down the grid, so whatever tops it is written first, above everything else.
Only the closing letter of the word that follows is wanted, not the word itself.

blocks.note: the closing letter of the word, sitting on top of the column
a mote is a speck of dust, as in the mote in your eye

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a pudding being decorated. The definition is a four-word idiom because English has no tidy single verb for overdoing a display of feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: lay it on thick → EMOTE: both describe overplaying an emotional display, and the verb is what critics reach for when an actor overdoes a scene.

clue.text: Elephant in bunk?

blocks.note: the male of the species — the same word covers a male whale, seal or moose, so this is one example of a class
bunk is nonsense, talk not worth listening to, and that is the sense the second definition wants

explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions dressed as one picture, joined by an 'in' that asserts nothing and only holds the sentence up.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephant → BULL is the male of the species, a definition by example; bunk? → BULL in its slang sense, nonsense not worth hearing.

clue.text: Shot down, completely unacceptable

blocks.note: the noise a gun makes, and a word for the shot itself
a lift or a machine that is down has stopped working

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot down' reads as one phrase, an argument demolished, and the two words belong to different halves of the build.
explanation.definitionFit: completely unacceptable → BANG OUT OF ORDER: British slang in which 'bang' is an intensifier meaning utterly, and behaviour out of order has crossed a line.

clue.text: With flexible back in exercise, stretch out – slight stretch?

indicators.note: Something flexible bends into whatever shape is asked of it, and so do the four letters beside it.
The back of a word is its final letter, the one bringing up the rear.

blocks.note: the clue's own opening word, its four letters put in a new order
the rear letter of the word 'exercise'
to stretch out on a sofa is to lie on it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch' appears twice and means something different each time: once the wordplay for the last chunk, once the definition. That is a setter's liberty, deliberately taken.
explanation.definitionFit: slight stretch? → WHITE LIE: stretching the truth is the idiom for lying, and the answer is the small harmless kind told to spare someone's feelings.

clue.text: After returning, record filled in by unknown emigrant

indicators.note: Coming back means retracing your steps, so the letters that follow are read from their far end.
A gap that is filled in has something dropped into it, so a letter goes inside the other piece.

blocks.note: a tape is a recording, and it is laid down the other way round
x is the unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a traveller home again and filling in a form, which lets the definition sit at the very end looking like the last word of a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: emigrant → EXPAT: an expatriate is someone settled outside their own country, which is what emigrating makes of a person; the clipped form is everyday English.
